title: Values, names, and surprising mutation

exercises.title: Find and fix the bug
exercises.prompt: A settings reader uses config[:send_email] || true. A report groups items using Hash.new([]). Explain the two independent bugs and repair both.

exercises.title: Change one condition
exercises.prompt: You dup a hash containing an array, then append to the copied array. What happens to the original? How would you avoid shared nested state?

trace.title: Variable name
trace.detail:
# Start with this

A Ruby variable points to an object. Assigning it to another variable usually copies the reference, not the object.

## See the difference

```ruby
a = [1]
b = a
b << 2
# a and b both see [1, 2]

b = [9]
# b now points somewhere else. a still sees [1, 2].
```

```text
Before reassignment:   a ─┐
                         ├──> [1, 2]
                      b ─┘
After reassignment:    a ────> [1, 2]
                      b ────> [9]
```

## One Ruby rule that surprises Java developers

Only `nil` and `false` are false in a condition.

`0`, `""`, and `[]` are all true.

A setting may correctly contain `false`. `settings[:enabled] || true` loses that choice.

Use `settings.fetch(:enabled, true)` when the default should apply only if the key is missing.

## Names and values

A symbol often acts as a label: `:status`. A string holds text: `"waiting"`.

Neither one is a security check.

Older books mention `Fixnum` and `Bignum`. In Ruby 2.7, their shared public class is `Integer`.

## Remember

Ask two questions: “Did I change the object?” and “Did I point this variable at another object?”

trace.title: Follow the middle steps
trace.detail:
Draw two arrows to the same array before the append. After second is reassigned, draw its arrow to a new array.

The first arrow did not move.

Hash.new([]) uses one shared default object and does not insert missing keys when you read them.

The block form above creates and stores a separate array for each new key. dup copies only one level; nested arrays can still be shared.

trace.title: Check the result
trace.detail:
A method ending in ! often warns about a surprising or dangerous variant; it is not a universal promise of mutation.

Read the method contract. freeze is also shallow unless you freeze nested objects yourself.
